questions.prompt: An HTTP/1.1 client pipelines two requests on one connection. The first response is slow. What ordering does the server have to preserve?

choices.text: Send complete responses in the order their requests arrived.
Send complete responses in application-completion order regardless of request order.
Interleave body bytes from both responses using request paths to distinguish them.
Send the second response first as long as each response supplies Content-Length.

questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 pipelined responses must be sent in request order. It does not provide HTTP/2-style interleaved streams.

sources.title: RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1
sources.claim: HTTP/1.1 permits persistent connections and pipelining but pipelined responses are sent in request order; connection limits are implementation choices.

questions.prompt: A page negotiates HTTP/2 and requests many resources over one TCP connection. How are the response messages represented?

choices.text: Each response must finish before any later response can start on that connection.
Each stream needs its own TCP connection even when the protocol is HTTP/2.
All response frames share one stream, with URLs identifying their message boundaries.
Frames for distinct streams can be multiplexed on that connection.

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes frames belonging to different streams over a connection. It remains TCP-based and does not require one connection per response.

sources.title: RFC 9113: HTTP/2
sources.claim: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a TCP connection, compresses fields, applies flow control and negotiates limits on concurrent streams.

questions.prompt: One HTTP/3 QUIC stream loses data while another has deliverable data. Which property helps the second stream?

choices.text: Loss on one QUIC stream necessarily blocks byte delivery on every other stream.
Each QUIC stream has completely separate connection bandwidth and congestion control.
Independent stream delivery avoids TCP-wide delivery blocking from that loss.
HTTP/3 must finish each response before transmitting frames for the next request.

questions.explanation: QUIC streams have independent delivery, avoiding the TCP ordering dependency across streams. Loss recovery and shared congestion constraints still exist.

sources.title: RFC 9114: HTTP/3
sources.claim: HTTP/3 maps HTTP onto QUIC streams with independent delivery and transport stream limits; it does not eliminate congestion or application dependencies.

questions.prompt: An interviewer says every browser always opens exactly six connections per host. What is the strongest correction?

choices.text: Every HTTP version mandates exactly six parallel transport connections per origin.
Connection limits are client policies, not a universal rule across HTTP versions.
HTTP/2 fixes concurrency at six streams even when peers negotiate a higher limit.
HTTP/3 permits only one active request stream because it uses one connection.

questions.explanation: The protocols do not establish a universal six-connection rule. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use streams with negotiated or transport limits, and client policies vary.

questions.prompt: An HTTP/1.1 response includes `Connection: close`. What does that signal about reuse?

choices.text: The connection is not retained for later requests after this response.
The response can be reused until its cache lifetime expires, regardless of the connection signal.
Only pipelining stops; later sequential requests must reuse that same open connection.
The connection remains reusable because HTTP/1.1 persistence cannot be disabled.

questions.explanation: Close signals ending the connection rather than persistent reuse. It is not a cache directive or an HTTP version upgrade.

questions.prompt: An HTTP/2 connection experiences missing TCP bytes. Why can other streams be delayed despite frame multiplexing?

choices.text: HTTP/2 serializes every response body in the original request order.
Multiplexing applies only to headers, so body frames cannot use concurrent streams.
Every stream has its own TCP ordering buffer so only the affected stream can wait.
TCP delivers ordered bytes, so missing data can hold up later bytes for all streams.

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 removes application-level response serialization but runs over an ordered TCP byte stream. TCP loss can therefore delay frames from otherwise independent streams.

questions.prompt: A team considers HTTP/1.1 resource loading. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Persistent HTTP/1.1 connections cannot be closed until the entire browser session ends.
Exactly six connections is a protocol requirement.
Persistent connections can carry later requests.
Pipelined responses retain request order.
Pipelining creates independently interleaved response streams.

questions.explanation: a: A connection can close earlier; persistence is not a browser-session lifetime guarantee. b: It is not a universal HTTP/1.1 requirement. c: HTTP/1.1 supports persistent reuse by default unless closure is signaled. d: The server must send responses in that order. e: HTTP/1.1 does not provide HTTP/2 stream framing.

questions.prompt: An HTTP/2 performance review discusses multiplexing. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Multiplexing guarantees unlimited server concurrency.
Distinct streams can share one TCP connection.
TCP loss can delay delivery across streams.
A stream identifier separates concurrent messages.
HTTP/2 uses QUIC instead of TCP by definition.

questions.explanation: a: Limits and server capacity still constrain work. b: HTTP/2 interleaves frames for streams. c: The transport still delivers an ordered byte stream. d: Frames identify the stream to which they belong. e: QUIC is the transport used by HTTP/3.

questions.prompt: An application migrates to HTTP/3. Which expectations are justified? Select all that apply.

choices.text: HTTP/3 maps requests onto QUIC streams.
Stream delivery avoids the TCP-wide ordering dependency.
HTTP/3 removes every application-level dependency between resource requests.
All congestion and bandwidth limits disappear.
Responses must be completed in request order.

questions.explanation: a: That is the protocol transport mapping. b: QUIC provides independent stream delivery. c: Transport stream concurrency does not remove application dependencies. d: QUIC still has transport constraints and congestion control. e: Separate request streams permit independent responses.

questions.prompt: A browser negotiates a modern HTTP protocol. Which concurrency assumptions hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: HTTP/3 stream availability depends on QUIC limits.
A client may impose additional scheduling policy.
Every HTTP version mandates six concurrent requests.
One multiplexed connection means unlimited bandwidth.
HTTP/2 peers can limit concurrent streams.

questions.explanation: a: The transport restricts how many streams can be opened. b: The protocol does not force unlimited request scheduling. c: No such universal cross-version mandate exists. d: Streams still share network capacity. e: SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS advertises a limit.
